latin: Cella ad tabulātum ēvecta<sup>1</sup>, adulēscēns valvam<sup>2</sup> aperit<sup>3</sup>. Equus et amīcus ē carcere suō<sup>4</sup> ērumpunt<sup>5</sup>.
Equum firmiter tenē! Cave<sup>6</sup> nē strepat nēve<sup>7</sup> inquilīnōs<sup>8</sup> excitet dum<sup>9</sup> in locō ancipitī<sup>10</sup> sumus.
Haec verba prōferēns adulēscēns jānuam quamdam cautissimē<sup>11</sup> uncō<sup>12</sup> aperīre cōnātur<sup>13</sup>.
Īrāscitur amīcus, equum tamen mūtum cōgēns<sup>14</sup>: «Nōlō, inquit, fūrtī<sup>15</sup> cōnscius esse<sup>16</sup>».
Ēsto<sup>17</sup> quiētus! Nihil fūrābimur. Nihil inhonestī agēmus. Tibi posteā rem explicābō.
Equum per faucēs<sup>18</sup> angustās prōpellunt. Tandem in cellam quamdam balneāriam perveniunt.
Nunc praecipuē auxilium tuum necessārium est.
latinAccented: Cella ad tabulā́tum ēvécta<sup>1</sup>, adulḗscēns valvam<sup>2</sup> áperit<sup>3</sup>. Equus et amī́cus ē cárcere suō<sup>4</sup> ērúmpunt<sup>5</sup>.
Equum fírmiter tenē! Cave<sup>6</sup> nē strepat nēve<sup>7</sup> inquilī́nōs<sup>8</sup> éxcitet dum<sup>9</sup> in locō ancípitī<sup>10</sup> sumus.
Haec verba prṓferēns adulḗscēns jā́nuam quamdam cautíssimē<sup>11</sup> uncō<sup>12</sup> aperī́re cōnā́tur<sup>13</sup>.
Īrā́scitur amī́cus, equum tamen mūtum cōgēns<sup>14</sup>: «Nōlō, inquit, fūrtī<sup>15</sup> cṓnscius esse<sup>16</sup>».
Ēsto<sup>17</sup> quiḗtus! Nihil fūrā́bimur. Nihil inhonéstī agḗmus. Tibi pósteā rem explicā́bō.
Equum per faucēs<sup>18</sup> angústās prōpéllunt. Tandem in cellam quamdam balneā́riam pervéniunt.
Nunc praecípuē auxílium tuum necessā́rium est.
english: The cabin having arrived at the floor, the young man opens the door. The horse and the friend [come out] of their prison (burst out).
Hold the horse firmly! [Make sure] (beware) [that] it doesn't make a racket and that it doesn't wake the tenants while we are in [a tricky situation] (a two-headed place).
Saying these words, the young man tries with [the greatest] (the most) precautions [to pick] (with a hook to open) [a] (certain) front door.
The friend gets angry, but nevertheless [keeps the horse quiet] (silent forcing): “I don't want, he says, to be [an accomplice to] a theft.”
Be calm! We are not going to do anything (we will steal nothing). We are not going to do anything dishonest. [I will tell you] later (thing I will explain).
There! The door is open: let's go in!
They push the horse through a narrow corridor (plural). Finally they reach a (certain) bathroom.
Now above all your help is necessary.

footnotes: Cella evecta: another ablative absolute! Evecta, perfect passive participle of eveho = ex + veho (-is, -ere, vexi, vectum, to carry [by means of a vehicle], to carry upwards).
Valva. We already had porta, the gate of a city, and janua, the door of a house. Valva designates the door in general, or even the valve (valve in mechanics and diode in radio-electricity).
Aperio, -is, -ire, aperui, apertum, to open. Not to be confused with operio, same conjugation, which means to cover, to cover over.

Suus, sua, suum, is the possessive adjective corresponding to the reflexive pronoun se (sui, sibi). Both normally refer to the subject of the clause, as we told you yesterday (L. 45, N. 2). If it is not the subject, then the genitive ejus of the demonstrative adjective-pronoun of reference is, ea, id is used to replace the possessive pronoun (see E. 44, P. 5).
Erumpo, -is, -ere, erupi, eruptum = ex + rumpo (lit.: to come out by breaking, to burst out).
Caveo, -es, -ere, cavi, cautum, to take care. Example: Cave canem!, beware of the dog (see figure); Cave ne cadas, be careful not to fall.
Neve = et ne, just as neque = et non.

Inquilinus, -a, m. or f., inhabitant, tenant, comes from the same root as incolere, to inhabit. The inhabitant of a country is called incola, -ae, m. — Strepo, -is, -ere, strepui, intransitive verb (no direct object), without supine, gave strepitus, -us, m., din. In Latin there are different words to represent the different kinds of noise: sonitus, -us, m., noise in general; crepitus, -us, m., crackling (also an unseemly noise); tonitrus, -us, m., noise of thunder, etc.
Dum + ind. = while; dum + subj. = until.
Anceps, ancipitis, adj., two-headed, in other words, of which one does not know which end to take. You already saw it in L. 31, P. 4: anceps erit exitus.

Cautus is the perfect participle of caveo (vid. sup., N. 6), whence the adverb caute, cautiously, and its superlative cautissime. Do not forget the pronunciation: kawtousss, kawéo — and remember that U and V were formerly represented by the same letter.
Uncus, -i, m., the hook; uncatus or uncinatus, bent, hook-shaped (unciform).
Conor, -aris, etc. + inf., to try (to do something).
Cogo, -is, -ere, coegi, coactum (cum + ago), to force.
Furtum, -i, n., theft, from fur, furis, m., thief; furari, to steal, whose future you will find in the following sentence.

Conscius (from cum + scire) is the opposite of nescius (ignorant). Note also that conscius is in the nominative, although it is in an infinitive clause. You know that the infinitive clause has its subject in the accusative (and the same goes for the predicate of the subject if the verb in the infinitive is a verb of state). But here the infinitive clause is incomplete: conscius, which can have no antecedent other than the subject of the MAIN CLAUSE, must agree with it, and therefore be in the nominative. On the other hand one would say dico me conscium esse, for in that case the infinitive clause is complete: subject me (and no longer ego understood), which can only be in the accusative, whence conscium, predicate, also in the accusative.
Esto!, be!; estote!, be (pl.)!, future imperative of the verb esse.
If you have forgotten fauces, refer to L. 40, P. 7 and N. 9.
comments: Sentence 2. Have you acquired the habit of mentally pronouncing quadragesimae quintae in Latin, and not 45 in English? Do not forget that ordinal number adjectives are declined (here gen. sg.)... and certain cardinal adjectives too.
Note (P. 6) tulit, perfect of that famous irregular verb fero, fers, ferre, tuli, latum, to carry.

latin: Amīcus certus in rē incertā cernitur.
Estne vir ille lēctiōnis 45ae et sequentium, ā quō adulēscēns auxilium petīvit, amīcus certus?
Hoc sciēs postquam tōtam fābellam lēgerīs.
Sine dubiō adulēscēns in locum ancipitem eum indūxit.
Nōnne rēs est incerta equum ad tabulātum quīntum pēgmate scansōriō dūcere?
Ergō sī in tālī cāsū auxilium alterī tulit, certus est amīcus.
Ita nōn arbitror. Adulēscēns equum fūrātus est: is nōn est amīcus certus quī fūrtī cōnscius est.
Quī equum fūrābitur, is in carcerem cōnjiciētur.
Quae cum ita sint, nescīs cujus sit equus quem adulēscēns surripuit.
latinAccented: Amī́cus certus in rē incértā cérnitur.
Estne vir ille lēctiṓnis 45ae et sequéntium, ā quō adulḗscēns auxílium petī́vit, amī́cus certus?
Hoc sciēs postquam tōtam fābéllam lḗgerīs.
Sine dúbiō adulḗscēns in locum ancípitem eum indū́xit.
Nōnne rēs est incérta equum ad tabulā́tum quīntum pḗgmate scansṓriō dū́cere?
Ergō sī in tālī cāsū auxílium álterī tulit, certus est amī́cus.
Ita nōn árbitror. Adulḗscēns equum fūrā́tus est: is nōn est amī́cus certus quī fūrtī cṓnscius est.
Quī equum fūrā́bitur, is in cárcerem cōnjiciḗtur.
Quae cum ita sint, nescīs cujus sit equus quem adulḗscēns surrípuit.
english: One recognizes a sure friend in [a tricky situation] (an uncertain thing).
Is the man of lesson 45 and the following ones, whom the young man asked for help, a sure friend?
You will know when you have read the whole story.
Without [any] doubt the young man [put him] in a tricky situation (led).
Isn't it [a risky] (uncertain) business to take a horse to the fifth floor by lift?
So, if in such a case he helped the other, he is a sure friend.
[I don't think so] (thus I do not think); the young man stole the horse; he who is the accomplice of a theft is not a sure friend.
[Whoever] (he who) steals a horse will be thrown into prison.
[Under these conditions] (which things since thus they are), you don't know to whom the horse belongs that the young man stole.
